planting.note: Root stem-tip cuttings in moist perlite or water and set plants out after the last frost into rich, well-drained soil in part shade to bright, filtered shade; deeper shade intensifies the magenta cast of the veining while hot direct sun can bleach and scorch the leaf surface.

directions: Set rooted cuttings into humus-rich, evenly moist soil once nights stay warm, choosing a part-shade to bright-shade spot where the leaf color reads most vividly. 'Brilliantissima' forms a dense, rounded mound of glossy, deep crimson-to-purple leaves shot through with hot pink veining, giving it a hotter, more saturated look than the plain species. Pinch stem tips through the growing season to keep the mound tight and to delay the small, inconspicuous flower spikes that can make older stems leggy. Lift and pot up stock cuttings before frost to carry the color through winter indoors as a houseplant.

common_name: Purple Lady Bloodleaf (Dark Purple Beefsteak Plant)

planting.note: Root stem-tip cuttings and transplant after the last frost into consistently moist, loamy soil in bright indirect light or part shade; 'Purple Lady' holds its near-black purple color best out of hot midday sun and makes a good trailing edge for containers and hanging baskets.

directions: Plant rooted cuttings into rich, consistently damp soil after danger of frost has passed, siting in indirect light or part shade for the deepest color. 'Purple Lady' is a lower, spreading selection of bloodleaf with a creeping-to-drooping habit and small, glossy leaves in a uniform deep purple that reads almost black in low light, making it a strong front-of-border or basket-spiller foliage plant rather than an upright accent. Water regularly, since it does not tolerate prolonged drying between waterings as well as some other bloodleaf types. Overwinter as a houseplant in bright indirect light north of zone 10, where it can persist for several years as a long-lived container specimen.

planting.note: Root stem-tip cuttings and set the compact plants out after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade; 'Wallisii' stays low and dense, making it a reliable dark-foliage edging plant for shaded bedding lines and container rims.

directions: Plant rooted cuttings into humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade after the last frost, spacing closely for a solid dark edging band. 'Wallisii' is the dwarfest common bloodleaf selection, forming a compact, low mound of small, rounded leaves in a near-black purple that holds its intensity in filtered light better than in deep shade or hot sun. Shear or pinch lightly through the season to keep the habit tight and to encourage denser branching from the base. Take fall cuttings to keep stock plants going indoors over winter, since the dwarf habit also makes it an easy small houseplant.
